title: Links & Anchors
summary: A link takes someone to another page, file, or place in the current page.

subtopics.title: The document frame
subtopics.explanation: `About us` creates a link to a page on the same site. The `href` value is the destination, and the text is what people activate. It is like a sign with both a direction and a readable label. The destination should work when opened directly too. For example, use `/account` for a route on the same site and a full URL for a different site. In practice, use a fragment link to jump to a heading whose ID remains unique on the page.

subtopics.title: Important pieces
subtopics.explanation: A URL can be a full address such as `https://example.com` or a path such as `/about`. A path stays within the current site. It is like using a street address or a room number in the same building. Choose the form that matches whether the destination is internal or external. For example, a link to `#pricing` works when the page contains a matching unique element ID. In practice, give repeated navigation links enough context to distinguish their destinations.

subtopics.title: Page information
subtopics.explanation: A fragment such as `#contact` jumps to an element whose `id` is `contact`. It is like a bookmark inside a long document. Use a unique ID and make sure the destination heading is visible after the jump, especially when a fixed header could cover it. For example, write “Read the refund policy” when that is the link destination. In practice, a download link should name the file or explain what will be downloaded.

subtopics.title: Content structure
subtopics.explanation: Descriptive link text tells people what will happen, such as “Read the return policy.” It is like labeling a sign with the destination instead of “go there.” Avoid vague text such as “click here,” which is difficult to understand when links are read out of context. For example, use a button to submit a form; use a link to open a destination. In practice, use rel protection when opening an external destination in a new tab.

subtopics.title: Good habits
subtopics.explanation: Opening a new tab changes browser behavior and can disorient people. Use it only when there is a clear reason, and explain the behavior when it may surprise someone. It is like opening a second book without closing the first. Native links preserve expected keyboard and browser actions. For example, if a new tab is necessary, make that behavior clear to the person activating the link. In practice, verify a route works after refresh, not only after client-side navigation.

foundations.overview: A link lets a person move to another page, another site, or a place within the current page. The `<a>` element uses `href` to name its destination. Think of it like a sign that points to a real place. Write link text that describes the destination, and use buttons for actions that change the current page rather than navigate.
foundations.whyItMatters: Links are a core way people navigate and share the web. Useful labels, stable destinations, and expected browser behavior make those paths reliable.
commonUseCases: Navigate to another page in the same site.
Jump to a section in a long help article.
Link to an external policy or service.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A clickable span is equivalent to a link.
commonMisconceptions.reality: An anchor provides keyboard behavior, destination semantics, and browser actions by default.

commonMisconceptions.myth: The text “click here” is clear to everyone.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Links may be scanned out of context; their text should describe the destination.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Every link should open a new tab.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Unexpected tabs can disorient users; preserve normal navigation unless there is a clear reason.

visualExplorer.title: Anatomy of a hyperlink
visualExplorer.caption: From the href to the link text, each part of an anchor shapes where it goes, how it opens, and how accessible it is.

config.intro: A robust link is more than href plus text. Walk through the parts that make a link correct, safe, and accessible.

steps.name: Pick the href
steps.detail: Choose the destination: an absolute URL for external sites, a relative URL for internal pages, #id for in-page jumps, or mailto:/tel: for contact.

steps.name: Write descriptive text
steps.detail: The clickable text must describe the destination on its own — 'Read the setup guide', not 'click here'.

steps.name: Decide the target
steps.detail: Default opens in the same tab. Use target="_blank" only when a new tab is genuinely helpful, and tell the user it opens new.

steps.name: Secure new tabs
steps.detail: With target="_blank", add rel="noopener noreferrer" to block window.opener access and withhold the referrer.

steps.name: Add special behavior
steps.detail: Use the download attribute for files, or fragment ids for jump links. Always provide visible fallback (e.g., the email address).

steps.name: Check accessibility
steps.detail: Ensure the link is keyboard-focusable, not color-only, and flag new-tab/download behavior to users.

interactiveExamples.title: Internal, external, and contact links
interactiveExamples.explanation: A relative internal link, an external link opened safely in a new tab, and mailto:/tel: contact links — each with descriptive text.

files.index.html:
About this site · MDN docs (opens in new tab)

Questions? Email the team (hello@example.com) or call +1 (555) 123-4567.

interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: A nav with an internal link and an external link that opens in a new tab, plus an email link (opens mail client) and a tel link, all with descriptive text showing the address/number.

interactiveExamples.title: Fragment links and a download
interactiveExamples.explanation: A table-of-contents fragment link jumps to a section by its id; a download link suggests a filename. Click 'Jump to details' to scroll the section into view.

files.index.html:
Jump to details

Scroll down to see the jump in action…

Details

You jumped straight here using a fragment link.

Download note.txt

interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: Clicking 'Jump to details' scrolls to the Details section, which contains a working download link that saves a text file named note.txt.

codeLab.title: Fix the unsafe and vague links
codeLab.instructions: This snippet has an external link that opens a new tab without rel protection, a non-descriptive 'click here' link, and a missing fallback on a contact link. Make the new tab safe, write descriptive text, and show the email address.

files.index.html:
Read our policy: click here.

Get in touch: email.

codeLab.expectedOutput: The external link opens in a new tab with rel="noopener noreferrer" and descriptive text; the email link shows the address.

files.index.html:
Read our policy (opens in new tab).

Get in touch: email team@example.com.

hints: Any target="_blank" link should also have rel="noopener noreferrer".
Replace 'click here' with text that describes the destination on its own.
For mailto links, show the actual address as fallback for users without a mail client.

keyTakeaways: `About us` creates a link to a page on the same site.
A URL can be a full address such as `https://example.
A fragment such as `#contact` jumps to an element whose `id` is `contact`.
Descriptive link text tells people what will happen, such as “Read the return policy.
Opening a new tab changes browser behavior and can disorient people.
